stories.topic: The Percy Mistry Committee Was Offended By 'Zombie Banks'
stories.summary: Long ago, on a Percy Mistry committee on Bombay as an International Financial Center, Ajay and Percy were 'merrily bandying the word zombie bank around' when some committee members were genuinely offended, treating it as disrespectful. In fact, 'zombie firm' and 'zombie bank' are technical terms from the research on Japan's lost decades.
stories.insight: Technical vocabulary from one field can sound like insult in another. Part of building a serious commercial culture is making peace with cold, accurate language for failure — the discomfort with the word is itself a symptom of the sentimentalism that prevents reform.

stories.topic: The Vlogger Who Threw The Camera At The Wall
stories.summary: A creative friend asked Amit for advice about making a vlog. Amit, channeling his usual encouragement to creators, said 'throw things at the wall.' Five minutes later the friend called back: he had thrown the camera. 'So this is not always great advice.'
stories.insight: The throw-things-at-the-wall heuristic is metaphorical — try many ideas cheaply, see what sticks. The joke is a warning that even good advice needs interpretive context, and a corrective for the idea that maxims travel cleanly across people.

stories.topic: Montek Knew The Companies Act 2013 Was Missing Something
stories.summary: Montek Singh Ahluwalia, then deputy chairman of the Planning Commission, had asked the Ministry of Company Affairs to put a full bankruptcy code with collective creditor negotiation into the new Companies Act of 2013. They assured him they would. They didn't. When he later asked Ajay to check, Ajay confirmed from his 'fair share of bedtime reading of the Companies Act' that there were only trivial winding-up provisions and no real bankruptcy process.
stories.insight: Even cabinet-level promises by ministries are unreliable in the absence of a knowledge community to verify them. Reform requires people who actually read the laws — bedtime reading included — because well-meaning ministers cannot police the technical content themselves.

stories.topic: Jaitley's Question: 'Do We Have The Ability?'
stories.summary: In 2015, the budget speech mentioned a small-firms bankruptcy code from the MSME ministry. KP Krishnan went to Finance Minister Arun Jaitley and asked: rather than this narrow thing, shall we attempt a full bankruptcy code? Jaitley's reply was the right one: 'Do we have the ability? Do we have the teams?' Krishnan pointed to the FSLRC's track record of large complex laws and world-class drafting capacity. That conversation seeded the BLRC and ultimately the IBC of 2016.
stories.insight: Big reform requires both ambition and an honest answer to the capability question. Krishnan's 'yes, we can' was credible only because the FSLRC had quietly built the institutional muscle in advance — reform momentum is a function of latent capacity that was assembled years earlier.

stories.topic: Japan's 30-Year Misery From Zombie Banks Propping Up Zombie Firms
stories.summary: After 1986, Japan's Ministry of Finance and MITI orchestrated industrial policy that kept failing banks alive, which in turn kept failing firms alive. The presence of these zombies destroyed the profitability of healthy firms across the entire economy. The result was 30 years of lost economic dynamism — the cost of refusing to let things die.
stories.insight: The cost of avoiding short-term pain in the financial system can be measured in decades of lost growth. Mercy toward dead firms is cruelty to the living ones that cannot earn enough to invest.

recommendations.item: ifrogs.org papers and xkdr.org firms-finance research
recommendations.creator: IFRoGS and XKDR Forum
recommendations.context: The foundational corpus of bankruptcy and credit-risk research that grew out of the BLRC work and continues today.
recommendations.reason: The empirical and theoretical bedrock of the Indian bankruptcy reform debate — for anyone who wants to actually understand the IBC rather than opine on it.

recommendations.item: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Reforms in India
recommendations.creator: Susan Thomas (editor)
recommendations.context: An edited volume of papers on the Indian bankruptcy reform.
recommendations.reason: The standing reference work on the IBC's design and early performance — the kind of book that anchors a knowledge community around a reform.

recommendations.item: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Reforms in India: 10 Years After the IBC
recommendations.creator: XKDR Forum
recommendations.context: A forthcoming 2026 book project assembling fresh research a decade after the IBC was passed; an authors' meetup happens alongside the December emerging-markets conference.
recommendations.reason: A live attempt to reconstitute the bankruptcy research community in India — exactly the kind of knowledge-ecosystem activity Ajay argues the country needs more of.

recommendations.item: An Annotated Reading List on Indian Bankruptcy
recommendations.creator: The Leap Journal
recommendations.context: A 2018 curated reading list on the Indian bankruptcy reform.
recommendations.reason: A self-guided syllabus for serious readers who want to do the work rather than just talk about it.

recommendations.item: Indian Bankruptcy Reforms: Where We Are and How To Move Forward
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah and others
recommendations.context: State-of-the-art reviews on The Leap Blog from 2016, 2017, and 2018.
recommendations.reason: Annual snapshots that let you trace how the IBC's promise was eroded year by year — a model of serious public-domain commentary on a reform in flight.

recommendations.item: Code 2.0
recommendations.creator: Lawrence Lessig
recommendations.context: Lessig's argument that code (technical and legal) is the architecture that shapes behaviour.
recommendations.reason: Picks up the episode's central image — that we live 'in the shadow of the law' — and shows how every word of a statute, every line of code, is doing work to constrain or enable human action. Every word in a bankruptcy code matters.

recommendations.item: Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid
recommendations.creator: George Roy Hill
recommendations.context: The 1969 western about two outlaws on the run.
recommendations.reason: An offhand recommendation closing an episode about the death of firms — a film about the romance and finality of running out of road.

recommendations.item: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE episode laying the foundational history of finance.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it an episode he 'absolutely loves' and the foundation for everything that follows about firms, debt, and capital.

recommendations.item: How Family Firms Evolve (Episode 34, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An earlier EIE on family firms and how their obvious answers can be wrong.
recommendations.reason: Builds on the firms canon — required context for thinking about why so many Indian bankruptcies are essentially family-firm failures.

recommendations.item: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An EIE on centralised vs decentralised firm structures.
recommendations.reason: The companion idea that firms are not static; their internal architecture must evolve, or the bankruptcy court eventually picks them apart.

recommendations.item: Graduating to Globalisation (Episode 48, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An EIE on the importance of internationalisation.
recommendations.reason: Pairs with the firms-die-and-are-reborn theme — global competition is one of the great forces of creative destruction.

recommendations.item: Four Papers That Changed the World (Episode 41, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An EIE on four foundational economics papers, including Coase on firms and Hayek on prices.
recommendations.reason: Direct upstream of this episode — explains why firms exist and why prices, not central planners, allocate resources.

recommendations.item: The Nature of the Firm
recommendations.creator: Ronald Coase
recommendations.context: Coase's 1937 paper asking why firms exist at all in a market economy.
recommendations.reason: The starting point for any serious thinking about firms — including the question of when a firm has stopped earning its right to exist.

recommendations.item: The Use of Knowledge in Society
recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Hayek's 1945 paper on the price system as a bottom-up information mechanism.
recommendations.reason: The case against central planning, and therefore the philosophical foundation for letting failed firms die — the price signal that says 'this resource is better used elsewhere.'

recommendations.item: Zombie Firms and Creative Destruction (Episode 118, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A long-form Seen and Unseen conversation on zombie firms.
recommendations.reason: The deep dive on the same diagnosis Ajay revisits here — what zombie firms do to a healthy economy.

recommendations.item: The Importance of Finance (Episode 125, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: A Seen and Unseen episode on why finance matters for development.
recommendations.reason: Foundational listening for understanding why a working credit market — and therefore a working bankruptcy code — is not optional.

recommendations.context: A long Seen and Unseen with the senior bureaucrat behind the IBC.
recommendations.reason: The episode where Krishnan tells the story of how the 2015 budget paragraph became the full Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code — inside-baseball on Indian reform.

recommendations.context: A Seen and Unseen with one of the lawyers who was on the team that drafted the IBC.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on the design of economic policy.
recommendations.reason: Source of the input/output/outcome framework, the zero-base list of essentials for civilization, and much of Ajay's vocabulary in this episode.

core_ideas.concept: Schumpeterian Creative Destruction Requires Both Birth and Death
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's framing: progress through innovation depends on a continuous cycle in which new firms are born around new ideas and old firms die when they cannot keep up. The atoms — labour and capital — are not destroyed; they flow back into society and into healthier firms. To take an interest in firms is to take an interest in birth and death together. In the Hindu metaphor, you need Vishnu (preservation) and Shiva (destruction) both, or the universe is out of balance.
core_ideas.quote: The carbon and the hydrogen atoms inside you will go back into other forms of life. So there's a ceaseless concept of firm destruction and firm creation.

core_ideas.concept: A Firm Is A Recipe (DNA), Not An Identity
core_ideas.explanation: A firm consumes labour and capital and organises them in a particular way — that organisation is the firm's DNA, the recipe that turns inputs into output. It is easy to become emotional about a firm because we get emotional about creatures, but a recipe can simply be wrong, or the world can move on. Tata Steel of 2024 is unrecognisably different from Jamshedji Tata's original; that adaptation is admirable, but most firms will not pull it off, and they should be allowed to die.
core_ideas.quote: You should think of the ways of a firm as being the DNA of an organism.

core_ideas.concept: Limited Liability As A Cold Contract
core_ideas.explanation: A 15th–16th-century European invention: shareholders run the company as long as they service their debts. The day they default, they lose control and usually lose their equity capital, and the creditors take over the company under a brand-new balance sheet where the old equity is wiped out. There is nothing sentimental in this concept; the words 'limited liability company' already contain the entire bankruptcy machinery. Indian discourse routinely forgets this and reaches for 'stakeholder' language as a sign of feeble reasoning.
core_ideas.quote: It's a very dramatic fact about the concept of a limited liability company that shareholders are in charge as long as they are meeting their dues. The day they fail to pay, they're supposed to get thrown out.

core_ideas.explanation: Firms that are economically dead but kept alive by bad credit are called zombie firms; the banks that prop them up are zombie banks. Their cost is not borne by themselves — it is borne by the healthy firms whose margins they destroy and the investments those healthy firms can no longer fund. Japan's lost three decades after 1986 is the canonical case: zombies kept aloft by an industrial policy run by the Ministry of Finance and MITI shattered profitability across the whole economy.
core_ideas.quote: These firms that are dead men walking are called zombie firms.

core_ideas.concept: A Bankrupt Firm Is A Melting Ice Cube
core_ideas.explanation: Once a firm gets into trouble, the wheels come off fast. Insiders know first; key employees leave; suppliers hold up goods; maintenance is skipped; promoters start extracting cash. Every day of delay destroys intangible capital — the people, processes, IT, contracts, culture that often make the firm worth more as a going concern than as a pile of parts. Speed is therefore the central virtue of a bankruptcy process: slow down, and there is nothing left to save.
core_ideas.quote: Once a firm starts getting into trouble, it's a melting ice cube.

core_ideas.concept: Tangible vs. Intangible Capital And The Going-Concern Choice
core_ideas.explanation: A firm in distress can be liquidated (sell the factory, the office, the land — sum of the parts) or sold as a going concern (preserving the orchestration of people, processes, IT, contracts, culture). When intangible capital is still alive, going-concern value usually exceeds liquidation value; when delay has destroyed it, only liquidation remains. The committee of creditors must make this judgement coldly and commercially — it is a business decision, not a humanitarian one.
core_ideas.quote: If I liquidate the firm will I get 40, and if I sell the firm as a going concern will I get 70?

core_ideas.concept: Committee Of Creditors As The Decision Forum
core_ideas.explanation: When a firm defaults, all the creditors are pulled together into a committee of creditors that takes the powers of the equity-holders. Different creditors have different interests — secured creditors can torpedo a going-concern plan by walking off with their collateral; operational creditors are first-class business players; some want the longest game, some the fastest exit. They haggle, with super-majority voting (60% or 70%, not 51%), and arrive at a value-maximising answer. The mechanism only works if its members are commercially badass — and that is exactly what Indian financial firms, deeply bureaucratic, are usually not.
core_ideas.quote: You can imagine it requires really sophisticated business instincts and bargaining in the committee of creditors, which all too often doesn't happen in India.

core_ideas.concept: In The Shadow Of The Law
core_ideas.explanation: The deepest outcome of a good bankruptcy code is not the cases it resolves but the cases that never reach court because counterparties privately negotiate under the threat of the law. Borrowers know the consequence of default; lenders know their remedies; both behave better. Most disputes settle privately. The ratio of cases-in-court to cases-resolved-privately is therefore a reverse measure of legal health: in advanced economies most action happens in the law's shadow.
core_ideas.quote: Most cases actually the behavior of all counterparties is changed.

core_ideas.explanation: A classification scheme for evaluating any reform: inputs are the law and institutions (NCLT, IBBI, the law on paper); outputs are throughput numbers (cases initiated, recovery rates); outcomes are what we actually want (better credit discipline, higher leverage, healthier capital allocation). Ministers and journalists tend to celebrate inputs and outputs because they are visible, but only outcomes count. Education's parallel: schools are inputs, grades are outputs, learning is the outcome.
core_ideas.quote: Ultimately, we are about outcomes. We've got to get to the outcomes.

core_ideas.concept: Theory Of Change Requires A Knowledge Ecosystem
core_ideas.explanation: Reform is the output of a pipeline: data sets, researchers, papers, blog posts, op-eds, criticism — a public-domain ferment that gives ministers and joint secretaries something to read and react to. Ministers cannot generate knowledge; their job is to make decisions in the presence of it. India's bankruptcy reform briefly had this ecosystem, then it dissipated. The IBC is now stuck because there are 'maybe two papers in this field a year' when there should be twenty. A reform without a research community is a reform without a future.
core_ideas.quote: Knowledge ecosystems are something far different from the thought process and the capability.

core_ideas.explanation: Indian banks, especially PSU banks, have a single overriding instinct: do not recognise that a loss has taken place. Marking-to-market is weak; the loan stays on the books at 100 even when the asset is worth 30. Evergreening — lending the borrower the money to repay the previous loan — is the cheapest way to keep the lie alive. When such banks then sit on a committee of creditors, they vote to delay, schedule the next meeting next month, and the melting ice cube melts on. The bankruptcy code's dysfunction is largely downstream of bad banking regulation.
core_ideas.quote: For banks, there's really only one overriding objective: how to hide the bad news.

core_ideas.concept: Reduce Bank Voting Power In The CoC
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's heterodox proposal: until banking regulation is fixed, banks should be given less voting power in committees of creditors. Mutual funds, FIIs, NBFCs, insurance companies, private banks all behave more commercially; PSU banks bring their CBI-fearing tape-painting culture into the room. Reducing their weight is a second-best fix while the first-best (better banking regulation) is unavailable.
core_ideas.quote: Until banking regulation figures out its act, the voting power of banks in the committee of creditors should be cut.

core_ideas.explanation: When a promoter senses the end is near, they begin extracting cash — sometimes illegally — and plant 'poison pills': obscure contractual provisions, hidden traps, weird arrangements only they know how to defuse. A new buyer steps on a landmine three months later. India therefore blocks promoters from bidding for their own bankrupt company in the IBC. Ajay considers this overcorrection — promoters often have the deepest knowledge of the business and would bid highest — but acknowledges that under Indian rule of law the poison-pill argument has force.
core_ideas.quote: There can be all kinds of commercial contracts where there's one weird provision left in there where suddenly something bad happens and only the promoter knows.

core_ideas.concept: Why The IBC Is A C-Grade Project
core_ideas.explanation: The IBC sits inside layers of dysfunction: bureaucratic banks unable to make commercial judgements; the NCLT working as poorly as any Indian court; the IBBI whose 140 carefully-designed regulator sections were deleted and replaced by eight cut-and-pasted SEBI sections; corruption pressures on insolvency professionals; an absent rule of law overall. The original design was excellent; the operating environment grades it down to C-class. The cure is not to abandon it but to keep iterating — and to rebuild the knowledge community that has dissipated.
core_ideas.quote: India has a C-grade bankruptcy process. Like, it's there, and yeah, it's better to have it than not to have it, but it has many difficulties.

core_ideas.explanation: Kelkar-Shah's framework for prioritising reform: list the elements of public policy without which civilisation collapses — foreign policy, military, fiat money, criminal justice, police, courts, tax system, commercial law, financial regulation. These are the primal foundations. Limited reform energy and limited philanthropic capital should concentrate here before chasing more glamorous causes. India's tendency to disperse effort across many subjects is precisely what blunts the impact of any one of them.
core_ideas.quote: We like to zero-base and say, give me a list of the elements of public policy that are essential for civilization, that without that you will be in barbarism.

core_ideas.explanation: Reform momentum is non-linear: many policy projects moving in parallel — capital controls, equity markets, software industry, telecom — produced positive feedback that strengthened each individual project. When only a few policy projects are in motion (as today), each of them works less well because the supporting environment isn't being upgraded around them. The bankruptcy reform suffers in part because the parallel banking-regulation reform that should have accompanied it never happened.
core_ideas.quote: When many policy projects are moving, you get a virtuous cycle. It strengthens everything.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's escalating opening: 'Firms are awesome, firms are amazing, firms are edifying, firms are illuminating, and when firms are sexually aroused, firms are firm.' (Ajay laughs — Amit notes 'first time ever he laughed at one of my jokes.')
Amit on Ajay's mythological turn: 'Am I sitting with Ajay Shah or am I sitting with my friend Devdutt Pattanaik?'

Amit on Japan's zombies: 'Japan not only had zombie firms and zombie banks. They also made a lot of great zombie movies. And I am wondering if I should go back and look at them with new eyes — dead man walking, axe in hand, hand chopped off — to see if there is great metaphorical art being created and we are taking it at surface value.'
Amit, after a friend asked for vlogging advice, told him to 'throw things at the wall.' Five minutes later: 'The camera, bro.' Amit's verdict: 'So this is not always great advice.'
Amit imagining a poison pill: 'Like a rat trap in the corner office, under the chair, under the table.' He immediately adds: 'I'm joking.'
Ajay correcting Amit's pronunciation: 'Internationalization. But that's not how you say it. It's I-eighteen-N — and everyone else also.'

Amit on Indian commercial culture: 'It makes me deeply sad that something that you were involved in, that Susan was involved in, that Bhargavi was involved in — it's today being dismissed by some random uncle as third-rate.'
Amit's gloss after Ajay's bank-incentive critique: 'Sunlight is the best disinfectant.'
Vishnu and Shiva — Ajay's metaphor for the bankruptcy process: you need preservation (Vishnu) and destruction (Shiva) both, or the harmony of the world is incomplete.

Joseph Schumpeter — the great economist whose 'creative destruction' frames the entire episode: temporary monopolies for innovators, the death of firms that cannot keep up, the recycling of labour and capital.
Ronald Coase, 'The Nature of the Firm' — the foundational paper invoked when defining what a firm even is.
Friedrich Hayek, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' — invoked for the bottom-up price-system argument against central planning, and therefore against propping up failed firms.

Douglass North and Oliver Williamson — invoked for the institutional-economics view that institutions create the conditions under which complex contracts (like limited-liability bankruptcy) become possible.
'In the shadow of the law' — the technical phrase for private negotiations conducted with the law as backstop, used here as the slogan for what a working bankruptcy regime actually delivers.

SARFAESI Act 2002 — the first Indian milestone toward modern bankruptcy: it gave secured creditors a mechanism to seize collateral, but offered no collective negotiation forum and pushed everything toward liquidation.

FSLRC (Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission, Justice Srikrishna, 2011–2015) — produced the specialised bankruptcy code for financial firms and the institutional template for how to draft Indian regulators properly.
BLRC (Bankruptcy Law Reforms Committee), led by TK Viswanathan with Susan Thomas drafting — the body that produced the IBC of 2016.

NCLT, IBBI, IBC — the three acronyms of the Indian bankruptcy architecture: the National Company Law Tribunal (the court), the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (the regulator), and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (the law itself).
'Stakeholder' — Ajay flags the word as 'a sure sign of feeble reasoning' in the bankruptcy context, where what is needed is cold business reasoning, not humanitarian language.
Evergreening of loans — the Indian banking euphemism for lending fresh money to a defaulter so they can repay the previous loan, kicking the can down the road indefinitely.
Air India / Jet Airways / Vistara — Ajay's example of how propped-up zombie airlines drive ticket prices below sustainable levels and damage healthy carriers.
